what-nobody-taught-you/act-i-—-the-limit.title: Cognitive biases as features (why they exist)
what-nobody-taught-you/act-i-—-the-limit.description: Part of Act I — The Limits of the Instrument (you)Cognitive biases are often taught as a list of defects to be memorized and apologized for. A more useful framing is that they are features with a context: heuristics that were selected for speed, frugality, and survival in environments very unlike the ones we now inhabit. Gigerenzer's term for this is ecological rationality — a heuristic is not rational or irrational in the abstract, only better or worse matched to an environment. A rule like "trust familiar faces" performs well in a small band of known kin and poorly on the internet. The bias is real; the bug is the mismatch, not the machinery.The strongest version of the "feature" argument is error management theory: when the two ways of being wrong have unequal costs, selection should push you toward the cheaper error. If a rustle in the grass might be wind or a predator, a false alarm costs you a startle and a missed predator costs you everything. So over-detecting threats, agents, and patterns is correct calibration, not a flaw. The same asymmetry explains negativity bias, loss aversion, and why we see faces in clouds.This does not license complacency. The point of "features, not bugs" is about origin and function, not about current reliability: hardware tuned for immediate, personal, ancestral risks misfires on probabilities, large numbers, slow-moving hazards, and anonymous strangers — which is most of modern life. It also means biases do useful social work, buying credibility, consistency, and commitment that pure calculation cannot. The practical upshot is not to delete them (you can't) but to design around them: checklists, pre-commitment, base rates, and second opinions, all of which appear later in this book. Heuristic — a fast, frugal rule of thumb that ignores some information to decide quickly; accurate in some environments, systematically wrong in others. Ecological rationality (Gigerenzer) — the idea that a heuristic's rationality is relative to the structure of the environment it operates in, not to an abstract standard of optimality. Error management theory — the principle that when the costs of two error types are asymmetric, selection favors bias toward the cheaper error. Smoke detector principle — the tendency to set a threshold low, accepting many false positives to avoid a rare catastrophic false negative. False positive / false negative — respectively, reacting to something that isn't there and failing to react to something that is. Evolutionary mismatch — the gap between the environment a mechanism was shaped in and the environment it now runs in; the source of most "bias" as experienced today. Apophenia / hyperactive agency detection — the over-perception of patterns, conspiracies, or intentional agents in noise.

what-nobody-taught-you/act-i-—-the-limit.title: Dual-process theory
what-nobody-taught-you/act-i-—-the-limit.description: Part of Act I — The Limits of the Instrument (you)Dual-process theory holds that the mind runs two kinds of processing. System 1 (Stanovich and West's original term was Type 1) is fast, automatic, parallel, associative, and always on: it recognizes faces, completes phrases, reads a friend's mood, and produces gut reactions. System 2 (Type 2) is slow, serial, effortful, and rule-governed: it does long division, compares two job offers, or checks whether a vivid statistic is plausible. Kahneman popularized the pair as "thinking fast and slow." The labels are a useful fiction, not two organs in the skull — what's real is a spectrum of processing features (automatic vs. controlled, parallel vs. serial), which usually but not always travel together.The decisive asymmetry is not that one system is smart and the other dumb, but that System 1 generates and System 2 endorses or overrides. Impressions, intuitions, and impulses arrive unbidden; deliberate reasoning audits some of them. But System 2 is expensive and lazy — Fiske and Taylor's cognitive miser, Kahneman's law of least effort — so it intervenes only when load is low, stakes are high, or something feels off. Most of the time, a System 1 output is simply accepted as if it had been reviewed. This is the machinery behind attribute substitution (answering an easy question instead of the hard one asked) and the biases covered earlier: the biases are the defaults, not defects bolted on.Two cautions keep the framework honest. First, System 2 is not a reliable hero: much of its work is post-hoc justification of conclusions System 1 already reached, which is confabulation wearing a lab coat. Second, expertise can make System 1 trustworthy — a firefighter's sense that the floor is about to go is pattern recognition, not bias — so the goal is calibration, not suspicion of intuition as such. Practically, you exploit the theory by designing situations where the slow system gets a chance: checklists, pre-mortems, cooling-off periods, and deliberately fetching the outside view before a judgment hardens. Critics note the two "systems" don't always cluster as advertised, and single-process accounts exist; treat the division as a lens for predicting when reasoning will fail, not as a claim about brain architecture. Dual-process theory — the account that cognition draws on two functionally distinct modes of processing, differing in speed, effort, and control. System 1 / Type 1 processing — fast, automatic, associative, parallel, non-effortful; source of intuitions and impulses. System 2 / Type 2 processing — slow, deliberate, serial, effortful, rule-governed; capable of monitoring and overriding System 1. Cognitive miser — the tendency to expend as little mental effort as a situation seems to allow. Law of least effort — Kahneman's principle that, among accessible strategies, the least demanding tends to win. Override — System 2's rejection or correction of a System 1 output; rare relative to endorsement. Attribute substitution — silently swapping a hard question for an easier one that System 1 can answer. Reification warning — the caveat that "System 1" and "System 2" name patterns of processing, not discrete brain systems.

what-nobody-taught-you/act-i-—-the-limit.title: Epistemic humility + calibrated confidence
what-nobody-taught-you/act-i-—-the-limit.description: Part of Act I — The Limits of the Instrument (you)Epistemic humility is often confused with low confidence. It isn't. Humility is a claim about your process: that your beliefs are fallible, that your evidence is partial, and that you should be willing to revise. Confidence is a claim about a specific proposition: how likely it is to be true given what you now know. A person can be maximally humble and still say "I'm 97% sure" — provided they're right about 97% of the time they say it.That property has a name: calibration. A forecaster is calibrated when the events assigned probability p occur about p of the time. Being calibrated is not the same as being accurate — you can be well calibrated and ignorant (always saying 50/50), or badly calibrated and often right in a lucky, overconfident way. Calibration is the easier half to fix and the half most people never measure, because it requires keeping score. The practical discipline is unglamorous: state probabilities numerically, write them down, resolve them later, and compare. Vague verbal hedges ("I think," "probably") cannot be scored, and so cannot be improved — which is exactly why they're so comfortable. This is where epistemic humility plugs into the Bayesian machinery: a probability is a bet, and a bet you never settle teaches you nothing.The failure mode is asymmetric. Humans are, in aggregate, overconfident about hard questions and underconfident about easy ones — and the confidence gap widens as the topic gets more abstract and more socially rewarded to have an opinion on. Two habits correct for it. First, the outside view: before estimating anything, ask how often this class of thing happens, rather than reasoning forward from your own case (base rates beat narratives). Second, the reversal test: name in advance what evidence would change your mind. If nothing could, you're not holding a belief — you're holding an identity.Humility and calibration are therefore two halves of one skill: humility keeps you updating, calibration tells you how much to update. Neither is a personality trait; both are scores you can raise. The uncomfortable implication is that most of the confidence you display at work, in argument, and in your own head has never been audited — not because you're dishonest, but because you've never had a mechanism that returns the answer. Epistemic humility — the stance that one's beliefs are fallible and evidence is partial; a claim about process, not a low probability estimate. Calibrated confidence — confidence that matches reality: events assigned probability p occur roughly p of the time. Overconfidence / underconfidence — systematic mismatch in either direction between stated and realised accuracy; typically overconfident on hard items, underconfident on easy ones. Scoring rule (e.g. Brier score) — a numeric penalty for probabilistic forecasts that rewards stating your true probability rather than hedging; makes calibration measurable. Outside view — estimating from the base rate of a reference class rather than from the specifics of your own case. Reversal test — the practice of naming, in advance, the evidence that would change your mind; a belief that survives no possible evidence is not a belief but an identity.

what-nobody-taught-you/act-i-—-the-limit.title: How memory actually works (reconstruction)
what-nobody-taught-you/act-i-—-the-limit.description: Part of Act I — The Limits of the Instrument (you)Memory feels like a recording: you experience something, it gets stored, and later you play it back. Nearly every layer of that metaphor is wrong. What actually happens is closer to reconstruction — the brain stores fragments, gist, and cues, then rebuilds a plausible version of the past each time you remember it, using your current beliefs, expectations, and context as building materials. The result feels like playback precisely because the rebuilding is seamless and the seams are invisible from the inside.The process runs in stages: encoding (what gets in, shaped by attention and prior knowledge), consolidation (stabilising traces over hours, days, and years, heavily dependent on sleep), and retrieval (rebuilding a memory from partial cues). Crucially, retrieval is not read-only. Each act of recall makes the memory briefly malleable again — reconsolidation — so it can be re-stored in an altered form. Remembering is therefore a form of editing, and the edit is invisible.This explains a family of findings that recording models cannot: Bartlett's participants reshaping a foreign folk tale into something culturally familiar; Loftus's misinformation experiments, where a single misleading question alters what witnesses "saw"; false memories of entire events implanted by suggestion; and confabulation, where patients with brain damage report detailed recollections of things that never happened, without any sense of fabrication. Confidence is a poor guide here — vividly "remembered" events are often confidently wrong, which is why eyewitness certainty is a weak predictor of eyewitness accuracy.The practical upshot is a calibration rule. Treat memory as testimony from a witness with an agenda, not as footage. Write down decisions, numbers, and agreements while they are fresh; prefer contemporaneous records over retrospective ones; and when someone — including you — recalls a conversation with total clarity, ask what else that memory is consistent with, not just how sure they sound. Memory is not a filing cabinet. It is a prediction about the past, generated in the present. Encoding — the initial acquisition of information; selective, and shaped by attention and prior knowledge. Consolidation — the gradual stabilisation of a memory trace, dependent on sleep and repetition. Retrieval — the act of rebuilding a memory from partial cues rather than reading a complete stored record. Reconstruction — the constructive process by which fragments, gist, and schemas are assembled into a coherent recollection. Reconsolidation — the window after recall in which a memory can be modified before being stored again. Schema — an organised body of prior knowledge that shapes what is encoded, and what is filled in later. Confabulation — the production of detailed false memories without intent to deceive and without awareness of error. Misinformation effect — the alteration of a memory by post-event information, such as a leading question. Source monitoring — the process of judging where a memory came from; failures produce "remembering" things you only imagined. Flashbulb memory — a vivid, confidently held memory of a shocking event, which is typically no more accurate than ordinary memory.

what-nobody-taught-you/act-i-—-the-limit.title: Illusion of understanding + confabulation
what-nobody-taught-you/act-i-—-the-limit.description: Part of Act I — The Limits of the Instrument (you)Familiarity is not comprehension, but the mind rarely signals the difference. Ask someone to rate how well they understand how a zipper works, then ask them to explain it step by step — the rating collapses. This is the illusion of explanatory depth: we mistake the ability to recognise, name, and use a thing for the ability to describe its mechanism. Fluency does the work. A concept we've heard about many times feels known, and that feeling of knowing is produced by processing ease, not by any stored causal model we could actually unpack.Confabulation is what fills the gap when the machinery runs without the evidence. The brain has no direct readout of its own causes, so it manufactures a plausible story after the fact and presents it as introspection. Split-brain patients asked why they performed an action invented an explanation they could not possibly have had; participants in choice-blindness studies defend choices they never made. This is not lying — the storyteller believes the story. Damage to memory or to self-monitoring makes the effect dramatic, but the ordinary version is continuous with everyday life: you decide, then you explain the decision, and moral and political reasoning is especially prone to it.The practical consequence is that introspection is a poor instrument for auditing your own understanding. The reliable test is generation, not recognition: try to write the explanation out, or teach it to a novice, and see where the sentence stalls. "Could I explain this to someone else?" is a far stricter question than "Do I get it?" — and the stalling point is exactly where real learning starts. Illusion of explanatory depth — the systematic overestimation of how well you understand a mechanism, revealed when you are asked to explain it in detail. Confabulation — the production of a plausible but fabricated explanation for one's own behaviour, offered sincerely and without awareness of the fabrication. Introspection illusion — the mistaken belief that introspection gives privileged, reliable access to the causes of one's own judgments and actions. Processing fluency — the ease with which information is processed; it is misread as a signal of truth, familiarity, or understanding. Choice blindness — the failure to notice that a choice one is asked to justify is not the choice one actually made. Generative test — evaluating understanding by producing an explanation or prediction from scratch rather than by recognising a correct one.

what-nobody-taught-you/act-i-—-the-limit.title: Predictive processing - perception as hallucination
what-nobody-taught-you/act-i-—-the-limit.description: Part of Act I — The Limits of the Instrument (you)Perception feels like reception: light hits your retina, sound hits your ears, and the world is delivered to you like a photograph. Predictive processing says the traffic runs mostly the other way. Your brain constantly generates a top-down guess about what is out there — a model of the causes of its sensory input — and compares that guess against the signal coming up from the senses. What propagates upward is not the image itself but the prediction error: the part of the input the guess failed to account for. Perception is the guess, corrected.The striking implication is that ordinary perception and hallucination sit on the same continuum. Both are internally generated constructions; the difference is that perception is controlled by sensory input, while hallucination is not. You are, in Anil Seth's phrase, hallucinating all the time — it is just that when we agree about our hallucinations, we call it reality. Illusions are the leak in the system: the hollow-mask effect, the McGurk effect, and a shadowed surface that still looks white all reveal the prior winning against the evidence, because the brain has learned that its priors are usually the better bet.Two practical consequences follow. First, perception is inference — the same logic as Bayesian reasoning, with priors standing in for base rates — so it inherits the same failure modes. Strong priors make you fast and efficient most of the time and blind precisely when the world has changed. Second, if the brain builds experience from a model, then memory, imagination, and perception are drawing on the same machinery — which is why remembering is reconstruction and why you can confabulate a reason for an action you never chose. The instrument does not report the world; it renders one. Change blindness and inattentional blindness — you perceive a stable scene, but the model is filled in from expectation, not sampled continuously. Expectation effects — a wine labeled expensive tastes better; the prior is doing part of the tasting. Stereotyping and first impressions — priors about people operate exactly like priors about objects, and they resist disconfirming evidence for the same reason. Cross-cultural and expertise differences — different priors, different percepts from identical input. Predictive processing — The theory that the brain continuously generates top-down predictions of sensory input and updates them using the resulting prediction errors.Top-down prediction — An internally generated expectation about the causes of incoming sensory data, derived from prior experience.Prediction error — The mismatch between what the brain predicted and what the senses actually delivered; the main signal traveling upward in the hierarchy.Prior — A pre-existing belief or expectation that biases interpretation of new evidence, in perception as in Bayesian reasoning.Controlled hallucination — Perception understood as a hallucination that is continuously constrained and corrected by sensory input, as opposed to an uncontrolled one.Perceptual inference — The process of inferring the most likely external cause of sensory signals, analogous to Bayesian belief updating.Percept — The experienced result of the prediction-and-correction process; what you take to be the world.

what-nobody-taught-you/act-i-—-the-limit.title: Tying it all together
what-nobody-taught-you/act-i-—-the-limit.description: Part of Act I — The Limits of the Instrument (you)Act I opened with a claim that sounds like an insult and turned out to be an architecture: you do not perceive the world, you render it. Six sections later, that same sentence has been restated in six registers — perceptual, memorial, introspective, computational, evolutionary, statistical — and the point of this section is to stop treating them as six findings. They are one finding, viewed from six angles, and the angles fit together in a way that changes what "thinking better" can even mean.Predictive processing says perception is inference. Memory research says recall is reconstruction. The illusion-of-explanatory-depth work says understanding is often recognition wearing a costume. Dual-process theory says judgment is a fast guess audited by a slow and reluctant reviewer. Bias research says the guess is well-adapted to an older world. Calibration research says nobody ever checks the guess against outcomes.Notice what these have in common. Every one describes the same operation applied to a different input: build the most plausible model consistent with partial cues, then hand the model forward as if it were the thing it models. A percept is a prediction presented as a photograph. A memory is a reconstruction presented as footage. An explanation is a post-hoc story presented as introspection. A judgment is a heuristic presented as reasoning. Four inputs, one algorithm, one output format.The consequence is not that you are unreliable in four ways. It is that the four failures interlock.Here is the synthesis that none of the individual sections states on its own. Your errors are not merely committed; they are corroborated. Each faculty takes testimony from the others and files it as independent evidence.Consider a worked example. You leave a Monday meeting certain that the team agreed to launch in March, and reasonably sure you heard the finance lead endorse it. Three weeks later you restate the March date in another meeting with complete confidence, and when challenged, supply a crisp reason why March was chosen. The transcript says April, that the finance lead said nothing, and that the reason you gave was never mentioned by anyone.Trace the machinery. Perception rendered a plausible meeting from partial attention. Memory filed the rendering as an observation, because it has no tag distinguishing "I saw this" from "I constructed this." Introspection, asked why you believe March, generated a plausible motive and presented it as recall of your own reasoning — the choice-blindness effect in ordinary clothes. System 1 proposed the date; System 2 endorsed it because fluency felt like evidence. Nothing in that sequence is a lie, and no step contains an error large enough to trip an alarm. The error is distributed, and each component laundered the last one's output.The dashed line is the deep point, and it is where this book's account departs from the standard one. Source-monitoring failure is usually taught as a memory phenomenon. It is not. There is no provenance channel anywhere in the instrument: no metadata attached to a belief saying this came from the senses, this came from a schema, this came from a story I just generated. Perception, memory, and introspection all write to the same channel in the same format, and the format is "this is how it is." You cannot introspect your way to the source of a belief any more than you can taste the difference between a remembered taste and an imagined one.The second consequence follows directly. If every faculty reports in the same confident format, then felt confidence carries no information about where the content came from — it carries information about how fluently the content was generated. Confidence is a property of the rendering process, not a reading off the evidence. This is why vivid memories are often confidently wrong, why the illusion of explanatory depth survives until the moment you try to explain, and why overconfidence grows as questions get more abstract: fluency is easier to produce when nothing is testable.So epistemic humility and calibration are not two virtues but one loop with two halves, and only one half can run inside your head. Humility — the recognition that the model is a model — is a stance you can adopt unilaterally. Calibration requires something the instrument does not contain: resolved outcomes, arriving later, in the world.Every arrow in that diagram except the last one is inside your skull. The loop closes only if you carry the belief out of the head, let the world resolve it, and then — this is the step almost nobody performs — write down what happened and look. Unclosed, cognition is open-loop: it produces beliefs, acts on them, and never receives a correction signal specifically about its own reliability. That is not a character flaw. It is a missing wire.The four limits are not equally tractable, and the remedies differ in kind. Two are impossible to fix internally and must be worked around; two can be improved directly.Everything Act I licenses reduces to four habits, and they are the skeleton the rest of the book hangs on.Externalize. Because memory edits on recall and introspection invents causes, anything that matters must leave the head while it is fresh — decisions, numbers, criteria, agreements, and above all the reason you made a call. This is not neatness. It is the only way to compare what you believed against what you said.Generate. Replace "do I get it?" with "can I produce it?" Explanation is the strict test; recognition is the lax one. The sentence that stalls is the boundary of your actual knowledge.Score. Convert hedges into numbers and settle them. "Probably" cannot be graded, which is precisely why it is comfortable. This is the calibration loop, and it is the one mechanism that returns a verdict on the instrument itself.Design. Since biases are features tuned to a vanished environment, you cannot will them away — a strategy of "try harder to be unbiased" asks System 2 to supervise System 1 permanently, which is exactly the arrangement the law of least effort defeats. You can, however, change the environment the defaults operate in: checklists, pre-mortems, cooling-off periods, base rates fetched before the judgment hardens. Design the situation where the slow system gets a turn.Act I does not make you smarter, and it is worth being blunt that it cannot. It makes you a different kind of thing: an instrument that knows it has no self-audit and therefore builds one outside itself. The reader who finishes this act with the impression that human cognition is hopeless has taken the opposite lesson. The machinery is remarkably good — good enough to have kept your ancestors alive, good enough that a firefighter's gut reads a collapsing floor, good enough that most of what you believe is roughly true. Its failure mode is narrow and specific: it cannot see its own seams, and it will not tell you when it is guessing.That is the hinge. If the instrument renders a map and insists it is the territory, then every subsequent question — what makes a claim meaningful, how to weigh evidence, when to defer to someone else — is the same problem in a different costume. Act I establishes that the map is drawn, not photographed. Act II asks what it can and cannot be trusted to represent.Rendering — the instrument's output format: a constructed model presented in the same format as a direct report, with no marker distinguishing construction from observation.Provenance channel — the hypothetical signal that would tell you whether a given belief came from the senses, from memory, from inference, or from confabulation. It does not exist; all sources write to one channel in one format.Source monitoring (generalised) — ordinarily a memory concept, extended here to all cognition: failures arise because no faculty can identify where its content originated.Corroboration ring — the circular arrangement in which each faculty treats the others' generated output as independent evidence, so that a distributed error accumulates confidence rather than triggering a check.Open-loop cognition — belief and action with no returning signal about the instrument's own accuracy; the default state, since outcomes resolve outside the head and are rarely recorded.Calibration loop — the cycle of stating a probability, acting, letting the outcome resolve, and scoring it; the only feedback that measures the instrument rather than the world.Generative test — judging understanding by producing an explanation or prediction from scratch rather than by recognising a correct one.Cognitive prosthetic — an external structure (written record, checklist, scoring sheet, pre-mortem) that performs a function the instrument cannot perform internally.

what-nobody-taught-you/introduction/how-.description: Part of Introduction Complexity & emergence — why systems behave in ways no one designed Feedback loops (reinforcing vs. balancing) — the grammar of all systems Nonlinearity & tipping points — why small causes have huge effects Path dependence & lock-in — how history constrains the present (QWERTY, VHS) Emergent vs. designed order — Hayek's insight, applied everywhere Second-order effects — the consequences of consequences Goodhart's Law — when a measure becomes a target, it fails Survivorship bias — the invisible graveyard behind every success story Bayesian reasoning — updating beliefs with evidence, intuitively Base rates & the outside view — why we ignore the obvious Black swans & fat tails — distributions that break our intuitions Epistemic humility — calibrated confidence, knowing what you don't know Map vs. territory — models are not reality The replication crisis — how science actually self-corrects (and doesn't) Falsifiability & what makes a claim meaningful How memory actually works — reconstruction, not recording The illusion of understanding — we think we know more than we do Confabulation — the brain invents reasons post-hoc Cognitive biases as features, not bugs — why they exist Dual-process theory — fast vs. slow, and when each fails Theory of mind & its limits — modeling other minds Predictive processing — perception as controlled hallucination Collective action problems — why groups fail to do what's good for them Tragedy of the commons (and Ostrom's escape from it) Institutions & why they matter (North, Ostrom, Acemoglu) Legibility vs. tacit knowledge — why central planners fail (Scott) Social construction — what's real vs. what's agreed-upon Norms vs. laws vs. markets — three coordination mechanisms Moloch / multipolar traps — races to the bottom Deep time — geological scales that dwarf human history Exponential vs. linear intuition — why we misjudge growth The Lindy effect — why old things tend to survive Ergodicity — when averages lie about your actual fate Discounting & the far future — how we undervalue tomorrow The is/ought gap — you can't derive values from facts Moral luck — how much of morality depends on circumstance Veil of ignorance — Rawls' thought experiment as a reasoning tool The map of mental models — how to think about thinking Epistemology of disagreement — when to defer, when to hold firm These share a signature: they change how you see everything else. Learn feedback loops and you see them in politics, biology, relationships, markets. Learn base rates and you stop being fooled by anecdotes. Learn legibility and you understand why bureaucracies fail. They don't fit neatly into one discipline They're uncomfortable (they undermine confidence and ideology) They require abstraction that schools avoid They have no immediate "use" — their value is cumulative The single most valuable concept might be "you are running on outdated cognitive hardware in a complex world." Every topic above is a specific instance of that. A textbook that taught that — not as cynicism but as a toolkit — would be genuinely rare and genuinely useful.One thesis, threaded throughout:You are running on cognitive hardware built for a simpler world, living inside complex systems you didn't design, making decisions under irreducible uncertainty. Every concept here is a tool for seeing that more clearly.That thesis gives you a reason for every chapter. Nothing is trivia — each concept earns its place by illuminating some part of that sentence.Here's the key to making it feel woven rather than listed — three concepts recur in every act, deepening each time:Spine Act I Act III Act V Prediction/maps Brain predicts Systems surprise us Mental models as maps Uncertainty Biases distort Fat tails break models Ergodicity decides fate Coordination Theory of mind Emergent order Moloch & institutionsEach recurrence adds a layer. By Act V, the reader sees the same three ideas from five angles — that's what makes it click instead of just accumulate.Every chapter ends with a "Connects to" section pointing to 2–3 others. Examples: Base rates → connects to survivorship bias, Bayesian reasoning, outside view Goodhart's Law → connects to legibility, institutions, second-order effects Emergence → connects to feedback loops, coordination, social construction Predictive processing → connects to memory, confirmation bias, Bayesian brain This turns the book into a network, not a list. Readers can enter anywhere and follow threads. You before world — you can't trust your instruments until you've examined them Knowing before systems — you need epistemology before you can model anything Systems before coordination — coordination is a special case of systems (agents in a system) Synthesis last — you can't synthesize what you haven't assembled Act V should include a single capstone: "The Toolkit." A one-page visual map of all ~40 concepts, showing: The five acts as layers The three spines as vertical threads Arrows for cross-connections One image the reader can return to forever. That's the artifact that makes the book referenceable, not just readable.

info_showOrphanNodes.description: Show nodes that are not connected to any other nodes.

info_showAttachments.description: Show attachments like images and PDFs as nodes in the graph.

info_allowGlobalGraph.description: Allow the user to view the global graph of all nodes.

info_allowExpand.description: Allow the user to pop-out the graph view to take up the whole screen

info_attractionForce.description: How much should linked nodes attract each other? This will make the graph appear more clustered.

info_linkLength.description: How long should the links between nodes be? The shorter the links the more connected nodes will cluster together.

info_repulsionForce.description: How much should nodes repel each other? This will make disconnected parts more spread out.

info_centralForce.description: How much should nodes be attracted to the center? This will make the graph appear more dense and circular.

info_edgePruning.description: Edges with a length above this threshold will not be rendered, however they will still contribute to the simulation. This can help large tangled graphs look more organised. Hovering over a node will still display these links.

info_minNodeRadius.description: How small should the smallest nodes be? The smaller a node is the less it will attract other nodes.

info_maxNodeRadius.description: How large should the largest nodes be? Nodes are sized by how many links they have. The larger a node is the more it will attract other nodes. This can be used to create a good grouping around the most important nodes.
